story.headline: Himalayan flood toll passes 470
story.summary: A Nepal-Tibet glacial flash flood has killed at least 469 with 977 missing, as an overflowing barrier lake threatens a second wave.
story.display_body: The death toll from the Nepal–Tibet Himalayan flash flood passed 470 on Friday 28 August as a newly formed "barrier lake" began to overflow, forcing rescuers on both sides of the border to pull back. Nepal's prime minister's office reported 469 confirmed dead and 977 still missing, with about 1,550 people rescued; Chinese authorities put the Tibet toll at at least five with 558 missing. The disaster began Wednesday 26 August when a glacier collapsed and sent a torrent of ice, rock and mud down the valleys of Rasuwa district, burying villages and destroying roads, bridges and hydropower plants. The debris then trapped a river into a "barrier lake" (a natural dam of landslide rubble), which by Friday had swollen past 2.5 million cubic metres — up from 1.5–2 million a day earlier — and started breaking its bank, prompting China to fly in engineers for aerial surveys and 3D modelling while residents scrambled uphill. The Red Cross said more than 90,000 people have been affected and that relief deliveries are being blocked by the rising water.
story.why: it is one of the deadliest glacial-outburst floods on record, the kind of high-mountain cascade scientists warn is becoming more likely as Himalayan ice destabilises, and the still-swelling lake means the death toll and the danger have not peaked.

story.headline: CIA chief made secret Moscow visit
story.summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow, confirmed by Russia's intelligence chief, reportedly to warn Russia off NATO's east and over Iran.
story.display_body: CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow on Tuesday 25 August, and Russia's foreign-intelligence chief confirmed the meeting on Wednesday 26 August. Russia's SVR (foreign intelligence service) head Sergei Naryshkin said he met Ratcliffe in what the Kremlin called talks "between the intelligence services," not with President Putin, and gave no detail on content. According to the Wall Street Journal and Politico, citing unnamed sources, Ratcliffe warned Moscow against any escalation aimed at NATO's eastern members — especially the Baltic states — and pressed the Kremlin to scale back its military and financial support for Iran. The Kremlin dismissed reports of preparations to attack NATO allies as "scare stories," insisting it prefers to pursue its aims by peaceful means even as its "special operation" in Ukraine continues.
story.why: a face-to-face channel between the US and Russian spy chiefs, carrying an explicit warning over NATO's flank and over Iran, is a rare direct signal in a war where such contacts are scarce — though the substance rests on anonymous US-media accounts, not confirmed readouts.

story.headline: Norway's King Harald V dies at 89
story.summary: King Harald V of Norway died at 89 on 28 August and was succeeded by his son, who reigns as King Haakon VIII.
story.display_body: King Harald V of Norway died on the morning of Friday 28 August at the age of 89, and his son Crown Prince Haakon immediately succeeded him. The Royal Palace said the king "passed away peacefully at Rikshospitalet on Friday 28 August at 06:35." Europe's oldest reigning monarch, Harald had been hospitalised on 17 August with haemolytic anaemia (a condition in which red blood cells are destroyed abnormally fast); crowds had gathered and laid flowers after officials warned his condition had turned "extremely serious." He took the throne in January 1991 on the death of his father Olav V, was the first Norwegian-born king since the 14th century, and won lasting affection for his 2011 speech after the Anders Behring Breivik attacks that killed 77 people. He had consistently refused to abdicate, citing his lifelong oath to parliament; his son now reigns as King Haakon VIII.

story.headline: Trump renames Lake Ontario Lake America
story.summary: Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America on US maps, escalating his trade war with Canada.
story.display_body: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday 27 August directing federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," escalating his trade war with Canada. The order tells US agencies to adopt the new name on American maps, documents and databases, but Trump has no authority over Canada's share of the lake or to compel Canada, international mapmakers or any global body to follow suit. It mirrors the order he signed on the first day of his second term renaming the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America." Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, as did several US governors — Wisconsin's Tony Evers openly mocked it.
story.why: the gesture is legally hollow beyond US borders, but it signals the trade dispute with Canada is hardening into personal provocation rather than cooling.

story.headline: Dittli quits Le Centre for new party
story.summary: Vaud state councillor Valerie Dittli left Le Centre to found her own party, Mouvement liberal, and seek re-election amid a party funds dispute.
story.display_body: Vaud state councillor Valérie Dittli announced on Friday 28 August that she is leaving Le Centre to found her own party, "Mouvement libéral," and will run for a second term under its banner. In an interview with Le Temps she said cooperation with the cantonal party had become untenable — "there are no words to describe it" — and she moved pre-emptively, days before Le Centre's Vaud delegates were due to meet on Wednesday 2 September to decide whether to back her re-election bid. The break follows an accusation, first reported by RTS on Thursday 27 August, that Dittli had improperly accessed a party account and tried to withdraw more than 20,000 francs; she denies it, saying the money was campaign donations paid in by supporters, and is weighing legal action. The new movement gathers former Centre and former FDP (Liberal-Radical) members; the first round of the Vaud cantonal election is set for 28 February 2027.
story.why: it fractures the centre-right in Vaud months before the vote and turns a sitting cantonal minister's re-election into a contest between her personal vehicle and the party that put her in office.

story.headline: Campaign budgets set for 27 Sept vote
story.summary: Switzerland's Federal Audit Office published about 8 million francs of campaign budgets for the 27 September federal vote on two popular initiatives.
story.display_body: The Federal Audit Office published the campaign budgets for the 27 September federal vote on Friday 28 August: about 8 million francs in total across two popular initiatives. Voters decide on the neutrality initiative and a food/agriculture initiative on Sunday 27 September. Backers of the neutrality initiative have budgeted the most — 3.84 million francs, of which more than 2 million comes from former federal councillor Christoph Blocher, 1.3 million from Pro Schweiz and 50,000 from the SVP; the opposing camp reported 1.67 million (Economiesuisse 1.2 million, the SP 367,000, Operation Libero 100,000). On the food initiative the "no" camp holds the larger purse at 1.63 million, drawn mainly from meat- and dairy-sector associations and the farmers' union. The reported spend is roughly half the record 16.27 million francs declared for June's "No 10-million Switzerland" vote.
story.why: under Switzerland's transparency rules these declarations are the public's clearest read on who is bankrolling each side a month before the ballot.

story.headline: Hail storms batter Swiss regions
story.summary: Violent hailstorms swept western and northwestern Switzerland on 28 August, causing widespread damage but no reported injuries.
story.display_body: Violent thunderstorms with golf-ball-sized hail swept western and northwestern Switzerland on Friday 28 August, causing widespread damage but no reported injuries. The canton of Solothurn was hit hardest, with well over 200 damage reports by midday. In Aargau a truck tipped onto a delivery van on the A1 motorway near Birrfeld/Birrhard, four power pylons came down — one onto a house — and part of a gymnasium roof was torn off in Aarau; power was cut in several Fricktal communities and the Biel–Olten rail line was closed until about 14:00. Regional train line R55 near Nyon (VD) was also affected before the front moved east toward Zürich and Schaffhausen.

story.headline: Bern to cut Tamiflu stockpile
story.summary: The Swiss government plans to cut its mandatory Tamiflu pandemic reserve to about a quarter of its current size as expiring capsules are destroyed.
story.display_body: The federal government plans to cut Switzerland's mandatory Tamiflu stockpile to roughly a quarter of its current size, with millions of expiring capsules now being destroyed unused. The legally required reserve stands at 200 pallets — about 3,900 shipping cartons of oseltamivir (the antiviral sold as Tamiflu) — enough for a century at normal use, built up more than a decade ago on the assumption the drug would be handed out to the whole population in a pandemic. That never happened during COVID, and the batches are now expiring. The Federal Office of Public Health told SRF its reassessment shows the compulsory reserve can be reduced to about a quarter, with future supplies reserved for hospitalised patients and those at high risk of complications.
